ch21.title: The First Disciples and the Wedding at Cana
ch21.b002: Early on Saturday morning, February 23, A.D. 26, Jesus came down from the hills to rejoin John’s company encamped at Pella. When a boy hurt himself in a fall, Jesus cared for him and took him home to his parents in the near-by village. Andrew, the one of John’s followers most deeply impressed with Jesus, went along, and on the way back the two stopped for a short talk. Andrew said: “⟦Q 137:1.1⟧I have observed you ever since you came to Capernaum, and I believe you are the new Teacher, and though I do not understand all your teaching, I have fully made up my mind to follow you; I would sit at your feet and learn the whole truth about the new kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus welcomed him with hearty assurance as the first of his apostles, that group of twelve who were to labor with him in establishing the kingdom of God in the hearts of men.
ch21.b003: Andrew had a very able and enthusiastic brother named Simon, one of John’s chief supporters. As soon as they were back in camp, Andrew took Simon aside and told him what he had done. Said Simon: “⟦Q 137:1.3⟧Ever since this man came to work in Zebedee’s shop, I have believed he was sent by God, but what about John? Are we to forsake him?⟦/Q⟧” The two went at once to consult John. He was saddened at the thought of losing two of his ablest and most promising disciples, but he answered bravely: “⟦Q 137:1.3⟧This is but the beginning; presently will my work end, and we shall all become his disciples.⟦/Q⟧” Then Andrew drew Jesus aside and told him that his brother wished to join the service of the new kingdom. In welcoming Simon as his second apostle, Jesus said: “⟦Q 137:1.3⟧Simon, your enthusiasm is commendable, but it is dangerous to the work of the kingdom. I admonish you to become more thoughtful in your speech. I would change your name to Peter.⟦/Q⟧” The parents of the injured boy had begged Jesus to spend the night in their home, and he had promised to do so. Before leaving the brothers he told them, “⟦Q 137:1.4⟧Early on the morrow we go into Galilee.⟦/Q⟧”
ch21.b004: Two Brothers Come Back Too Late
ch21.b005: That night James and John, the sons of Zebedee, returned to the camp from their long and fruitless search for Jesus in the hills. When they heard Simon Peter tell how he and Andrew had become the first accepted counselors of the new kingdom, they were sad. They hurried to Pella and woke him from his sleep. “How is it,” they asked, “⟦Q 137:1.6⟧that, while we who have so long lived with you are searching in the hills for you, you prefer others before us?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered, “⟦Q 137:1.6⟧Be calm in your hearts and ask yourselves, ‘who directed that you should search for the Son of Man when he was about his Father’s business?’⟦/Q⟧” And he added: “⟦Q 137:1.6⟧You should learn to search for the secret of the new kingdom in your hearts and not in the hills. That which you sought was already present in your souls.⟦/Q⟧”
ch21.b006: Then, laying a hand on the shoulder of each, he told them that they had been with him in the spirit of the kingdom from the beginning, before the others had asked, and that they might even have been first before men had they not been away “⟦Q 137:1.6⟧engaged in a well-intentioned but self-appointed task of seeking for one who was not lost.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 137:1.6⟧In the coming kingdom, be not mindful of those things which foster your anxiety but rather at all times concern yourselves only with doing the will of the Father who is in heaven.⟦/Q⟧” James and John took the rebuke in good grace and were never again envious of Andrew and Simon. From that day the word apostle was used to set apart this chosen family of Jesus’ advisers from the great multitude of believing disciples. Late that evening the four talked with John the Baptist, and with tearful eye but steady voice the stalwart Judean prophet gave up two of his leading disciples to become apostles of the Galilean Prince of the coming kingdom.
ch21.b008: On Sunday morning, February 24, Jesus took leave of John by the river near Pella, never again to see him in the flesh. That day there was a great tumult in John’s camp, the first great division among his followers. One of them, Ezra, rejected the mild-mannered carpenter outright. “⟦Q 137:2.2⟧The Prophet Daniel declares that the Son of Man will come with the clouds of heaven, in power and great glory,⟦/Q⟧” he told his companions. “⟦Q 137:2.2⟧This Galilean carpenter, this Capernaum boatbuilder, cannot be the Deliverer.⟦/Q⟧” When John rebuked him, Ezra drew away with many disciples and went south, and they became a sect that believed in John but refused to accept Jesus.
ch21.b009: Meanwhile Jesus and his four apostles were well on the way toward Galilee. Before they crossed the Jordan, Jesus saw Philip of Bethsaida coming down the road toward them with a friend. Philip was on his way to John to learn more about the coming kingdom; his friend Nathaniel of Cana stayed behind to rest in the shade of a roadside tree. Peter took Philip aside, told him that the four of them had become associates of Jesus, and urged him strongly to join them. Philip was in a quandary. Without a moment’s warning, on a roadside near the Jordan, the most momentous question of his life had come up for immediate decision. At last Andrew suggested, “Why not ask the Teacher?” Philip went straight to Jesus and asked, “⟦Q 137:2.5⟧Teacher, shall I go down to John or shall I join my friends who follow you?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered, “Follow me.”
ch21.b010: Thrilled to have found the Deliverer, Philip hurried back to Nathaniel, who still sat under the mulberry tree turning over in his mind all he had heard of John, the coming kingdom, and the expected Messiah. Philip broke in upon his thoughts: “⟦Q 137:2.6⟧I have found the Deliverer, him of whom Moses and the prophets wrote and whom John has proclaimed.⟦/Q⟧” When Philip told him it was Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph the carpenter, Nathaniel asked, somewhat shocked, “⟦Q 137:2.6⟧Can any such good thing come out of Nazareth?⟦/Q⟧” Philip took him by the arm and said, “Come and see.” Jesus looked kindly into the face of this sincere doubter and said: “⟦Q 137:2.7⟧Behold a genuine Israelite, in whom there is no deceit. Follow me.⟦/Q⟧” Nathaniel turned to Philip: “⟦Q 137:2.7⟧You are right. He is indeed a master of men. I will also follow, if I am worthy.⟦/Q⟧” And Jesus nodded to him, saying again, “Follow me.”
ch21.b011: Now half of his future company of intimate associates was gathered. They crossed the Jordan, passed by the village of Nain, and reached Nazareth late that evening, where they spent the night with Joseph in Jesus’ boyhood home. The new associates little understood why their teacher took such care to destroy every trace of his writing that remained about the house.
ch21.b013: The next day Jesus sent his apostles on to Cana, for all of them had been invited to the wedding of a prominent young woman there, while he paid a hurried visit to his mother in Capernaum, stopping at Magdala to see his brother Jude. Hearing the apostles’ story, his brother Joseph had said: “⟦Q 137:3.2⟧Maybe, after all, Mother was right—maybe our strange brother is the coming king.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus reached Capernaum on Monday night and went straight to the home of Zebedee. All his friends saw a great and pleasant change in him. For years before his baptism he had grown more and more serious and self-contained; now he seemed lighthearted and joyful again, much as he had been in his early years at Nazareth, though there was about him something of majestic import.
ch21.b014: Mary was thrilled with expectation. She believed the promise of Gabriel was nearing fulfillment and that all Palestine would soon be stunned by the miraculous revelation of her son as king of the Jews. But to all the questions of his mother, James, Jude, and Zebedee, Jesus only replied with a smile: “⟦Q 137:3.5⟧It is better that I tarry here for a while; I must do the will of my Father who is in heaven.⟦/Q⟧” On Tuesday they all went over to Cana for the wedding of Naomi and Johab the son of Nathan, set for the following day. In spite of Jesus’ warnings, they quietly spread the news that they had found the Deliverer. Mary had not been so joyous in years; she traveled to Cana in the spirit of a queen mother on her way to see her son crowned.
ch21.b016: By noon on Wednesday almost a thousand guests had come to Cana, more than four times the number invited. It seemed more like a public reception for Jesus than a wedding, and everyone rejoiced when he agreed to lead the wedding procession. But as the day wore on, he grew more and more aware that the people, and especially his family and his six apostles, expected him to announce his kingdom by some startling supernatural sign. Early in the afternoon Mary and James came to ask at what point in the ceremonies he planned to manifest himself as the “supernatural one.” They saw at once that they had aroused his characteristic indignation. He said only: “⟦Q 137:4.4⟧If you love me, then be willing to tarry with me while I wait upon the will of my Father who is in heaven.⟦/Q⟧” For several hours Mary was much depressed. Jesus withdrew for an hour alone, then returned lighthearted and joyous. Just before the wedding supper he called the six together and said earnestly: “⟦Q 137:4.6⟧Think not that I have come to this place to work some wonder for the gratification of the curious or for the conviction of those who doubt. Rather are we here to wait upon the will of our Father who is in heaven.⟦/Q⟧”
ch21.b017: Before the supper was over, the servants brought the bridegroom’s father the disconcerting news that the wine was running short. When the guests were strolling in the garden, the bridegroom’s mother confided to Mary that the wine was gone. Mary answered confidently: “⟦Q 137:4.7⟧Have no worry—I will speak to my son. He will help us.⟦/Q⟧” She found Jesus standing alone in a corner of the garden. “⟦Q 137:4.8⟧My son, they have no wine.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered, “⟦Q 137:4.8⟧My good woman, what have I to do with that?⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 137:4.8⟧But I believe your hour has come; cannot you help us?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus replied: “⟦Q 137:4.8⟧Again I declare that I have not come to do things in this wise.⟦/Q⟧” Breaking into tears, Mary begged him: “⟦Q 137:4.8⟧But, my son, I promised them that you would help us; won’t you please do something for me?⟦/Q⟧” And Jesus said: “⟦Q 137:4.8⟧Woman, what have you to do with making such promises? See that you do it not again. We must in all things wait upon the will of the Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧”
ch21.b018: Mary was crushed. As she stood motionless before him with tears streaming down her face, the human heart of Jesus was overcome with compassion for the woman who had borne him. Bending forward, he laid his hand tenderly on her head and said: “⟦Q 137:4.9⟧Now, now, Mother Mary, grieve not over my apparently hard sayings, for have I not many times told you that I have come only to do the will of my heavenly Father? Most gladly would I do what you ask of me if it were a part of the Father’s will—⟦/Q⟧” And Jesus stopped short; he hesitated. Mary seemed to sense that something was happening. Leaping up, she threw her arms around his neck, kissed him, and hurried off to the servants’ quarters, saying, “⟦Q 137:4.9⟧Whatever my son says, that do.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said nothing. He realized that he had already said—or rather desirefully thought—too much.
ch21.b019: Near at hand stood six stone waterpots, each holding about twenty gallons of water for the final purification ceremonies of the feast. The bustle of the servants around these great vessels caught Jesus’ attention, and going over, he saw that they were drawing wine out of them by the pitcherful. Of all the people at the marriage feast of Cana, Jesus was the most surprised. Then he remembered the warning of his Personalized Adjuster in the hills, that no power could deprive him of the creator prerogative of independence of time. Power transformers, midwayers, and all other required personalities had been gathered near the water, and in the face of the expressed wish of the Universe Creator Sovereign, there was no escaping the instantaneous appearance of wine; the Adjuster had signified that it was in no way contrary to the Father’s will. Yet this was in no sense a miracle. No law of nature was modified or transcended; nothing happened but the abrogation of time. When the servants carried the new wine to the ruler of the feast, he called to the bridegroom and said: “⟦Q 137:4.15⟧It is the custom to set out first the good wine and, when the guests have well drunk, to bring forth the inferior fruit of the vine; but you have kept the best of the wine until the last of the feast.⟦/Q⟧”
ch21.b020: Mary and the disciples rejoiced at what they took for an intentional miracle, and the people looked at him with awe and believed in him as the Messiah. But he was sorely perplexed, knowing that they believed only because of the unusual thing they had just seen. Again he withdrew for a time to the housetop to think it over. He understood now that he must be constantly on guard lest his sympathy and pity lead to repeated episodes of this kind. Nevertheless, many similar events occurred before he took final leave of his life in the flesh.
ch21.b022: Though many guests stayed for the whole week of festivities, Jesus and his six apostles left very early the next morning without saying good-bye to anyone. On the way he warned them to say nothing about the turning of water into wine and advised them to avoid Sepphoris and Tiberias in their future work. That evening, after supper in the home of Zebedee and Salome at Bethsaida, there took place one of the most important conferences of his whole earthly career. But when Jesus tried to make clear to them who he was, what his mission was, and how it might possibly end, they were stunned. Even Peter was speechless; only the deep-thinking Andrew dared to answer. Seeing how fixed their ideas of the Jewish Messiah were, Jesus sent them to bed and walked with his brother Jude, who had followed him from Cana. Before leaving for his home at Magdala, Jude said with much feeling: “⟦Q 137:5.2⟧My father-brother, I never have understood you. … I heard the voice at the Jordan, and I am a believer in you, no matter who you are.⟦/Q⟧”
ch21.b023: That night Jesus did not sleep. Wrapped in his evening garments, he sat by the lake shore thinking until dawn. In those long hours he came to see clearly that he would never be able to make his followers see him as anything other than the long-expected Messiah. Though he was not the Davidic type of Messiah, he was truly the fulfillment of the prophecies of the more spiritually minded of the olden seers. Never again did he wholly deny that he was the Messiah; he left the untangling of this complicated situation to the Father’s will. At breakfast he found his friends a cheerless group. He told them that it was the Father’s will that they wait in the neighborhood until John’s preaching was finished, and he sent them back to their nets while he went with Zebedee to the boatshop.
ch21.b025: Jesus’ first public appearance after his baptism was in the synagogue at Capernaum on the Sabbath, March 2, A.D. 26. The story of the Jordan, now added to by the fresh news from Cana, packed the building to overflowing. The six apostles sat in the seats of honor with his brothers James and Jude, and his mother sat in the women’s section. The whole congregation was on edge, waiting for some extraordinary display of supernatural power. They were disappointed. Jesus read a passage from the Prophet Isaiah, handed back the roll, and before sitting down said simply: “⟦Q 137:6.3⟧Be patient and you shall see the glory of God; even so shall it be with all those who tarry with me and thus learn to do the will of my Father who is in heaven.⟦/Q⟧” The people went home wondering what it all meant.
ch21.b026: That afternoon he took the apostles, with James and Jude, in a boat a little way down the shore, anchored, and talked with them about the coming kingdom. He told them to return to their usual work as if nothing had happened, and to tell no man about him. “⟦Q 137:6.5⟧Remember that my kingdom is not to come with noise and glamor, but rather must it come through the great change which my Father will have wrought in your hearts.⟦/Q⟧” He warned them against false hopes: “⟦Q 137:6.5⟧Make no mistake; we go forth to labor for a generation of sign seekers.⟦/Q⟧” When they came back to land that evening, Jesus stood by the water’s edge and prayed: “⟦Q 137:6.6⟧My Father, I thank you for these little ones who, in spite of their doubts, even now believe.⟦/Q⟧”
ch21.b028: For four long months, March through June, the waiting went on. Jesus held more than a hundred long and earnest, yet cheerful, sessions with the six and his brother James. By day they went about their ordinary work, Jesus himself setting the example by returning to the boatshop; night after night they sat at his feet. Nothing, absolutely nothing, miraculous happened. Peter kept urging Jesus to begin preaching in Galilee while John still preached in Judea, but the answer was always: “Be patient, Simon. Make progress.” Mary’s faith, raised so high at Cana, sank to new depths, and she could only repeat: “I cannot understand him.” Jesus also taught them their attitude toward the Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, Zealots, and Herodians: “⟦Q 137:7.5⟧We are seeking to win all of them, but we are not of any of them.⟦/Q⟧” In later years the apostles looked back on these four months as the most precious and profitable of all their time with the Master. He taught them only as much as they could assimilate.
ch21.b029: On Tuesday, June 18, as Jesus worked in the boatshop, Peter brought him the news of John’s arrest. Jesus laid down his tools once more, took off his apron, and said: “⟦Q 137:8.2⟧The Father’s hour has come. Let us make ready to proclaim the gospel of the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” That was his last work at the carpenter bench. On the Sabbath, June 22, he stood in the pulpit of the Capernaum synagogue and preached his first great sermon on the kingdom:

ch21.b030.en: “I have come to proclaim the establishment of the Father’s kingdom. And this kingdom shall include the worshiping souls of Jew and gentile, rich and poor, free and bond, for my Father is no respecter of persons; his love and his mercy are over all. … My kingdom is not of this world. … If you would but believe that my Father loves you with an infinite love, then you are in the kingdom of God.”

ch21.b031: All who heard him were astonished. About a third believed the message even though they could not fully understand it; about a third prepared in their hearts to reject so purely spiritual an idea of the kingdom; and the rest could not grasp his teaching at all, many truly believing that he “was beside himself.”
ch22.title: The Twelve Are Gathered
ch22.b002: On the afternoon of the day he preached the sermon on “The Kingdom,” Jesus called the six apostles together and began to disclose his plans for visiting the cities around and about the Sea of Galilee. His brothers James and Jude were not called to this conference, and they were very much hurt. Up to this time they had regarded themselves as belonging to his inner circle, but Jesus planned to have no close relatives among the apostolic directors of the kingdom. This failure to include them, together with his apparent aloofness from his mother ever since the experience at Cana, was the starting point of an ever-widening gulf between Jesus and his family, a gulf that would not be fully closed until after his death and resurrection. His mother wavered constantly between a fluctuating faith and hope and growing emotions of disappointment, humiliation, and despair. Only Ruth, the youngest, remained unswervingly loyal to her father-brother. If a prophet is not without honor save in his own country, he is not without understanding appreciation save in his own family.
ch22.b003: The next day, Sunday, June 23, A.D. 26, Jesus gave his final instructions to the six. They were to go forth two and two and teach the glad tidings of the kingdom. He forbade them to baptize and advised against public preaching; for a season, and for many reasons, he wanted them to acquire practical experience in dealing personally with their fellow men. Though this was something of a disappointment, they saw at least in part the reason for it and set out in good heart: James and John to Kheresa, Andrew and Peter to Capernaum, Philip and Nathaniel to Tarichea. Before they went, Jesus announced that he desired to ordain twelve apostles to continue the work of the kingdom after his departure, and he authorized each of them to choose one man from among his early converts. John asked whether these six new men would share all things equally with those who had been with him since the Jordan. Jesus replied: “⟦Q 138:1.2⟧Yes, John, the men you choose shall become one with us, and you will teach them all that pertains to the kingdom, even as I have taught you.⟦/Q⟧”
ch22.b004: The six did not separate until they had talked long about this instruction. Andrew’s counsel finally prevailed. In substance he said that the Master was right, that they were too few to encompass the work, and that he had shown great confidence in them by intrusting them with the choosing of the new apostles. Still, as they parted that morning, there was a bit of concealed depression in each heart. They knew they would miss Jesus, and this was not the way they had pictured the kingdom of heaven being inaugurated. Meanwhile Jesus went over to Nazareth to visit Joseph and Simon and other members of his family, doing everything humanly possible, consistent with his dedication to the Father’s will, to keep their confidence and affection. He thought much, too, about John, now in prison. It was a great temptation to use his potential powers to release him, but once more he resigned himself to “wait upon the Father’s will.”
ch22.b006: When the two weeks were over and the six gathered again at the home of Zebedee, they all wanted to talk at once. The first tour had been eminently successful. They had discovered the great value of direct and personal contact with men, and they came back more fully realizing that religion is purely and wholly a matter of personal experience. They had begun to sense how hungry the common people were for words of religious comfort and spiritual good cheer. Andrew took charge, calling on them one by one, and each made his report to the Master and presented his nomination. After each name Jesus asked the others to vote, and so all six of the new apostles were formally accepted by all of the older six. Jesus spent a full day with them, listening to the details of their experiences, and they now saw the wisdom of laboring in a quiet and personal manner before launching any more pretentious public effort.
ch22.b007: Andrew had chosen Matthew Levi, the customs collector of Capernaum, whose office stood just east of the city near the borders of Batanea. Philip had chosen Thomas Didymus, a fisherman of Tarichea and onetime carpenter and stone mason of Gadara. James Zebedee had chosen James Alpheus, a fisherman and farmer of Kheresa, and John had chosen his twin brother, Judas Alpheus, also a fisherman. Peter had chosen Simon Zelotes, once a merchant and now a high officer in the patriotic organization of the Zealots, a position he gave up to join the apostles. Nathaniel had chosen Judas Iscariot, the only son of wealthy Sadducee parents of Jericho, who had disowned him when he attached himself to John the Baptist. He was looking for employment in these regions when the apostles found him, and it was chiefly because of his experience with finances that Nathaniel invited him. Judas Iscariot would be the only Judean among the twelve.
ch22.b008: The Call at the Toll House
ch22.b009: The next day Jesus and the six went to call upon Matthew. He was waiting for them, having balanced his books and made ready to turn the affairs of his office over to his brother. As they approached the toll house, Andrew stepped forward with Jesus, who looked into Matthew’s face and said, “Follow me.” And Matthew arose and took them all to his house. He told Jesus of a banquet he wished to give that evening for his family and friends, if the Master would consent to be the guest of honor, and Jesus nodded. After a noontide luncheon they went with Peter to call upon Simon the Zealot, whom they found at his old place of business, now kept by his nephew. When Peter led Jesus up to him, the Master greeted the fiery patriot and only said, “Follow me.”
ch22.b010: They returned to Matthew’s home and talked much of politics and religion until the evening meal. The Levi family had long been in business and tax gathering, and many of the guests were such as the Pharisees would call “publicans and sinners.” It was the custom in those days, when such a banquet was given for a prominent man, for anyone interested to linger about the room and watch the guests at meat and listen to the speeches, and most of the Pharisees of Capernaum came to observe Jesus. As the dinner went on, the joy of the diners mounted to heights of good cheer, and the onlookers grew cold in their hearts. At last one of the more malignant among them said to Peter, “⟦Q 138:3.6⟧How dare you to teach that this man is righteous when he eats with publicans and sinners and thus lends his presence to such scenes of careless pleasure making.⟦/Q⟧” Peter whispered the criticism to Jesus, and before the parting blessing the Master spoke to all. He was glad, he said, to witness their lightheartedness and social good cheer, but they should rejoice still more because many of them would find entrance into the coming kingdom of the spirit. Then he turned to those who stood about criticizing him in their hearts: “⟦Q 138:3.6⟧I have come to proclaim joy to the socially downtrodden and spiritual liberty to the moral captives. Need I remind you that they who are whole need not a physician, but rather those who are sick? I have come, not to call the righteous, but sinners.⟦/Q⟧”
ch22.b011: It was a strange sight in all Jewry, a man of righteous character and noble sentiments mingling freely and joyously with the common people, even with an irreligious and pleasure-seeking throng. Simon Zelotes wanted to make a speech, but Andrew, knowing that Jesus did not want the coming kingdom confused with the Zealots’ movement, prevailed upon him to keep silent. Jesus and the apostles remained that night in Matthew’s house, and as the people went home through the dark streets, they spoke of but one thing: the goodness and friendliness of Jesus.
ch22.b013: On the morrow the nine crossed by boat to Kheresa. The twin sons of Alpheus, James and Judas, were waiting on the shore, for they had been expecting them. James Zebedee presented the Master to the two fishermen, and Jesus, gazing on them, nodded and said, “Follow me.” That afternoon he instructed them fully concerning attendance upon festive gatherings, and he ended with these words: “⟦Q 138:4.2⟧All men are my brothers. My Father in heaven does not despise any creature of our making. The kingdom of heaven is open to all men and women. … Refuse not therefore to break bread with Pharisee or sinner, Sadducee or publican, Roman or Jew, rich or poor, free or bond. The door of the kingdom is wide open for all who desire to know the truth and to find God.⟦/Q⟧” That night, at a simple supper in the Alpheus home, the twins were received into the apostolic family. Later Jesus gave them a first lesson on the origin, nature, and destiny of unclean spirits, but they could not comprehend it. They found it very easy to love and admire Jesus but very difficult to understand many of his teachings.
ch22.b014: After a night of rest the eleven went by boat to Tarichea, where Thomas the fisherman and Judas the wanderer met them at the fisher-boat landing. In Thomas’s home near by, Philip presented Thomas, and Nathaniel presented Judas Iscariot, the Judean. Jesus looked upon Thomas and said: “⟦Q 138:5.1⟧Thomas, you lack faith; nevertheless, I receive you. Follow me.⟦/Q⟧” To Judas Iscariot he said: “⟦Q 138:5.1⟧Judas, we are all of one flesh, and as I receive you into our midst, I pray that you will always be loyal to your Galilean brethren. Follow me.⟦/Q⟧” Now they were twelve. Jesus took them apart to pray and to teach them of the Holy Spirit, but again each grasped only a fragment; always they tried to fit his new gospel into their old forms of belief. The next day he left them alone to become acquainted, and that evening he spoke to them of the ministry of seraphim.
ch22.b015: Back in Capernaum, Zebedee and Salome had gone to live with their son David so that their large home could be given over to Jesus and the twelve. There the Master spent a quiet Sabbath with his chosen messengers, outlining the plans for proclaiming the kingdom and warning them to avoid any clash with the civil authorities: “⟦Q 138:5.4⟧If the civil rulers are to be rebuked, leave that task to me. See that you make no denunciations of Caesar or his servants.⟦/Q⟧” That same evening Judas Iscariot took Jesus aside to ask why nothing was being done to get John out of prison. And Judas was not wholly satisfied with Jesus’ attitude.
ch22.b017: They were a varied company. Except for the Alpheus twins, all were graduates of the synagogue schools, thoroughly trained in the Hebrew scriptures, and seven had studied in the schools of Capernaum, the best in all Galilee. When they were called “ignorant and unlearned,” it meant only that they were laymen, untrained in the lore of the rabbis. The apostles learned from Jesus about the kingdom of heaven, and Jesus learned much from them about the kingdom of men. It is an eloquent testimony to his charm and righteousness that, though he repeatedly dashed their hopes of personal exaltation, only one deserted him.
ch22.b018: Andrew, at thirty-three, was the oldest and the ablest. Excepting oratory, he was the peer of his associates in almost every ability; the others soon called him by a term the equivalent of Chief. He was a man of clear insight and firm decision whose strength was his superb stability. He was the best judge of men among them; he knew that trouble was brewing in the heart of Judas Iscariot when none of the others suspected anything, but he told no one his fears. He was never jealous of his brother’s eloquence and never minded being introduced as “Simon Peter’s brother.” Andrew admired Jesus for his consistent sincerity, his unaffected dignity.
ch22.b019: Peter was thirty, married, with three children, a man of impulse and an optimist who persisted in speaking without thinking. He asked more questions than all the other apostles put together. He was a brave soldier before a frontal attack but withered and shrank before ridicule. Yet his faults were of the head and not of the heart; his great strength was loyalty, and he truly loved Jesus. The trait he most admired in the Master was his supernal tenderness, and he never forgot the lesson about forgiving the wrongdoer, not only seven times but seventy times and seven.
ch22.b020: The two sons of Zebedee Jesus nicknamed “sons of thunder.” James, thirty years old, was much like Andrew except for periodic upheavals of fiery temper and spells of unaccountable silence. Of all the twelve he came nearest to grasping the real import of Jesus’ teaching, and he most admired the Master’s sympathetic affection. John, at twenty-four the youngest, was dependable, prompt, and courageous, though marked by an inordinate but usually well-concealed conceit. He served as Jesus’ personal agent in dealing with his family. The Master’s love and unselfishness so impressed him that this “son of thunder” became at last the “apostle of love.”
ch22.b021: Philip, twenty-seven and the steward, lacked imagination but was methodical and thorough; only a few times in four years did he fail to have food on hand. He was always wanting “to be shown,” and he would interrupt even Jesus’ most profound discourses with apparently foolish questions, yet Jesus never once rebuked him. He had the great and rare gift of saying, “Come”—“Come and see.” He worshiped the Master’s unfailing generosity. His friend Nathaniel, twenty-five, was the honest one, “without guile.” His weakness was pride; he had asked, “⟦Q 139:6.3⟧Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?⟦/Q⟧” but he reversed himself the moment he looked into Jesus’ face. He was the apostolic philosopher and probably the best storyteller among them, and he looked after the families of the twelve. He most revered Jesus for his tolerance.
ch22.b022: Matthew, thirty-one, was the only man of any means among them, and his fellows called him the “money-getter.” He gave practically the whole of his modest fortune to the work, but he gave it in the names of other believers, for fear they might regard his money as tainted. None of them ever knew, save Jesus, who knew all about it. It was the Master’s forgiving disposition that Matthew most appreciated. Thomas, twenty-nine, had the one truly analytical mind of the twelve; he was the real scientist of the group. He was suspicious and moody, but when he was outvoted, he was always the first to say, “Let’s go!” He revered Jesus for his superbly balanced character.
ch22.b023: The Alpheus twins, James and Judas, twenty-six, were commonplace fishermen who understood very little of the philosophical discussions but gladly managed the crowds and ran every errand. They were “⟦Q 139:9.5⟧the least of all the apostles⟦/Q⟧”; they knew it and felt cheerful about it. Jesus does not look down upon littleness, only upon evil and sin. Simon Zelotes, twenty-eight, was a fiery agitator who could bring a wavering soul into the kingdom in about fifteen minutes, but four years were too short a time to change a Jewish nationalist into a spiritually minded internationalist. He admired the Master’s calmness, his assurance, poise, and inexplicable composure.
ch22.b024: And there was Judas Iscariot, thirty and unmarried, probably the best-educated man among them. He was a farseeing and able treasurer, and he was always financially loyal; money could never have been the motive for what he would later do. The apostles loved him; he was really one of them. But Judas did not really understand himself. He had been a spoiled only son, a poor loser, an expert at misinterpreting the words and acts of his friends. To Jesus, Judas was a faith adventure. From the beginning the Master understood the weakness of this apostle, but it is the nature of the Sons of God to give every created being a full and equal chance. The door of eternal life is wide open to all: “whosoever will may come.”
ch22.b026: Jesus had planned a quiet campaign of five months’ personal work, though he did not tell the apostles how long it would last. Early on the first day of the week, just as he was about to announce it, Simon Peter, James Zebedee, and Judas Iscariot came to speak with him privately. Peter made bold to ask, on behalf of the others, whether the time was not ripe to enter into the kingdom, whether it would be proclaimed at Capernaum or in Jerusalem, and when each of them would learn the position he was to occupy. He would have gone on, but Jesus raised an admonitory hand and stopped him. Beckoning the others to come near, he said: “⟦Q 138:7.1⟧My little children, how long shall I bear with you! Have I not made it plain to you that my kingdom is not of this world? … My friends, hear me once more. Banish from your minds this idea that my kingdom is a rule of power or a reign of glory. Indeed, all power in heaven and on earth will presently be given into my hands, but it is not the Father’s will that we use this divine endowment to glorify ourselves during this age.⟦/Q⟧”
ch22.b027: Once more they were shocked, stunned. Jesus sent them away two and two to pray and told them to return at noon. On that crucial forenoon each sought to find God and to cheer the other. When they came back, Jesus recounted for them the coming of John, the baptism in the Jordan, the marriage feast at Cana, the choosing of the six, and the withdrawal of his own brothers in the flesh, and he warned them that the enemy of the kingdom would seek to draw them away as well. Then the apostles all arose under Peter’s leadership to declare their undying devotion and to pledge their loyalty, as Thomas put it, “⟦Q 138:7.3⟧To this coming kingdom, no matter what it is and even if I do not fully understand it.⟦/Q⟧” They truly believed in Jesus, even though they did not fully comprehend his teaching.
ch22.b028: When Jesus asked how much money they had and what provision had been made for their families, it turned out they had hardly enough to maintain themselves for two weeks. “⟦Q 138:7.4⟧It is not the will of my Father that we begin our work in this way,⟦/Q⟧” he said. They would stay by the sea for two weeks and fish, and in the meantime, under Andrew’s guidance, they would organize themselves for the work ahead. “⟦Q 138:7.6⟧And then will you go forth to become fishers of men.⟦/Q⟧” They were greatly cheered; this was the first clear sign that he meant later to enter upon more public efforts. They fished in three groups, and Jesus went out with a different boat each night. Many of the boats they used had been built by his own hands, good and trustworthy boats. He was a good fisherman, a cheerful companion, and an inspiring friend. Said Matthew one day: “⟦Q 138:7.6⟧The more you understand some people, the less you admire them, but of this man, even the less I comprehend him, the more I love him.⟦/Q⟧”
ch22.b030: The apostles organized themselves early. Andrew was chairman and director general; Peter, James, and John were the personal companions of Jesus, to attend him day and night and accompany him on his vigils of prayer; Philip was steward; Nathaniel watched over the families of the twelve; Matthew was the fiscal agent; Thomas managed the itinerary; the Alpheus twins managed the multitudes; Simon Zelotes had charge of recreation and play; and Judas Iscariot, the treasurer, carried the bag. At this time, too, Jesus established a midweek holiday, usually Wednesday, and on that day he would generally go off by himself, saying: “⟦Q 138:6.2⟧My children, go for a day of play. Rest yourselves from the arduous labors of the kingdom and enjoy the refreshment that comes from reverting to your former vocations or from discovering new sorts of recreational activity.⟦/Q⟧”
ch22.b031: From about the middle of August, A.D. 26, they followed a plan of two weeks fishing and two weeks going out two and two to do personal work, and they kept it up for more than five months. Jesus went out with each pair in turn. He taught them to preach the forgiveness of sin through faith in God without penance or sacrifice, and he charged them not to speak of the work and imprisonment of John, of the voice at the baptism, or of the water and the wine at Cana. They labored in Capernaum, Bethsaida-Julias, Chorazin, Gerasa, Hippos, Magdala, Gadara, and many other towns and villages. John had taught “⟦Q 138:8.8⟧repentance—to flee from the wrath to come.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus taught, “⟦Q 138:8.8⟧Faith is the open door for entering into the present, perfect, and eternal love of God.⟦/Q⟧” The disciples saw that he had a profound respect for every human being he met. He would pause in a profound discourse to go out to the road and speak good cheer to a passing woman laden with her burden of body and soul, and he would interrupt a serious conference to fraternize with an intruding child. The apostles were at first shocked by his treatment of women, but they soon grew used to it; women, he made clear, were to have equal rights with men in the kingdom.
ch22.b032: It was a somewhat monotonous and grueling season. They grumbled and doubted, yet they endured the test. During these months Jesus’ entire family, except Ruth, practically deserted him. But to each apostle the Master became the best friend he had in all the world. In the dark hours of the trial and crucifixion it was this supreme sentiment of friendship-loyalty, and not his superb teachings or marvelous doings, that held them all, save Judas Iscariot, true to him. And so they went on in this simple manner until Sunday, January 12, A.D. 27, when Jesus called them together to ordain them as ambassadors of the kingdom.
